words.shortDefinition: The billing and capacity unit that determines the compute size and instance count available to hosted web applications.
words.simpleDefinition: An App Service plan defines the region, pricing tier (F1 free through Isolated v2), and number of VM instances that back one or more App Service apps. All apps sharing a plan share those resources. Scaling the plan scales every app on it.
words.longDefinition: An Azure App Service plan is the underlying infrastructure contract for App Service: it specifies the region, OS, pricing tier (Free, Shared, Basic, Standard, Premium, Isolated), and instance count that every App Service app sharing that plan runs on. The tier determines features — custom domains, TLS, autoscale, VNet integration, and deployment slots — and the per-instance VM size. You can host multiple apps on one plan for cost sharing, or isolate high-traffic apps on dedicated plans. Autoscale rules (metric or schedule based) change instance count at the plan level, and scaling out adds identical VMs rather than resizing. The Isolated tier runs inside an App Service Environment (ASE) for VNet-private, dedicated compute.
words.connector: Like a lease for a floor in an office building: the floor (plan) determines how many desks you have, and any number of tenants (apps) can share the space.
words.techContext: Moving the API and the admin portal onto the same Azure App Service plan reduced our hourly compute bill without affecting performance.
words.exampleSentence: We upgraded the Azure App Service plan from B1 to P2v3 and turned on autoscale to handle the daily traffic spike.

codeExample.code:
az appservice plan create \
  --name prod-plan --resource-group myRG \
  --sku P2v3 --is-linux

words.etymology: Descriptive name: a 'plan' (subscription or contract) for the Azure 'App Service' hosting platform.

words.shortDefinition: A service that launches isolated containers on demand in seconds, with per-second billing and no cluster to manage.
words.simpleDefinition: It is the fastest way to run a container in Azure: you provide an image and resource requirements and the container starts in seconds on Microsoft-managed infrastructure. There is no cluster, no scheduler, and no persistent hosts to maintain. It suits short-lived jobs and lightweight workloads that do not need orchestration.
words.longDefinition: Azure Container Instances (ACI) provides hypervisor-isolated containers that start in seconds without provisioning VMs or managing a container orchestrator. You specify an image (from Azure Container Registry or any public registry), CPU and memory, environment variables, and optional persistent volume mounts (via Azure Files), and ACI handles placement, networking, and billing per CPU-second and GB-second consumed. Containers can be public- or private-network facing, support multi-container groups (sidecar patterns) on Linux, and integrate with virtual network injection for private access. ACI is ideal for burst processing, CI/CD tasks, event-driven batch jobs, and quick prototyping. For long-running, auto-scaling workloads you would graduate to Azure Container Apps or AKS.
words.connector: Like renting a van for one trip: the vehicle appears ready when you need it and disappears when you are done, no garage required.
words.techContext: Our nightly ETL pipeline submits Azure Container Instances jobs that fan out across images and terminate when each task finishes.
words.exampleSentence: The QA team runs smoke tests in Azure Container Instances so every pull request gets a fresh, isolated environment in under a minute.

codeExample.code:
az container create \
  --resource-group myRG --name job-runner \
  --image myregistry.azurecr.io/worker:latest \
  --cpu 1 --memory 1.5 --restart-policy Never

words.etymology: Descriptive: 'container' (Docker-style) + 'instances' (on-demand occurrences); Azure service launched in 2017.

words.shortDefinition: A fully managed serverless platform for deploying containerized services with built-in autoscaling, traffic splitting, and Dapr support.
words.simpleDefinition: It runs microservices and background jobs in containers without managing Kubernetes directly: you push an image and Azure handles scheduling, scaling to zero, and revision-based traffic splitting. KEDA drives scale-out on queue depth, HTTP traffic, or custom metrics. Dapr is optionally available for service discovery and pub/sub.
words.longDefinition: Azure Container Apps (ACA) is a serverless container platform built on Kubernetes and KEDA under the hood, exposing a simplified model that hides cluster management. Apps live in an environment (a shared VNet boundary and Log Analytics workspace); each app manages revisions, and traffic can be split across revisions for blue/green or canary deployments. KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling) powers scale rules based on HTTP concurrency, queue length, or custom metrics, including scaling to zero when idle. Dapr (Distributed Application Runtime) integrates for service-to-service invocation, pub/sub, state management, and secrets — all configured declaratively. Container Apps suits microservice APIs, event-driven workers, and long-running jobs with unpredictable or spiky load, sitting between ACI (one-off tasks) and AKS (full Kubernetes control).
words.connector: Like a smart apartment building where the landlord auto-assigns rooms, moves tenants based on demand, and provides shared plumbing — you just move in.
words.techContext: We deployed eight microservices to Azure Container Apps and let KEDA scale each one independently from zero based on Service Bus queue depth.
words.exampleSentence: Deploying the background processor to Azure Container Apps let it scale to zero overnight, cutting idle compute costs to nothing.

codeExample.code:
az containerapp create \
  --name api --resource-group myRG \
  --environment myEnv \
  --image myregistry.azurecr.io/api:latest \
  --target-port 8080 --ingress external

words.etymology: Descriptive name for a managed platform ('Apps') running 'container' images on Azure.

words.shortDefinition: A managed, geo-replicated private catalog for storing, securing, and distributing OCI images and Helm charts.
words.simpleDefinition: It is a private home for your Docker images and OCI artifacts inside Azure: you push images during CI and pull them in ACI, AKS, or Container Apps. It supports vulnerability scanning, geo-replication, and Tasks to build images in the cloud. Access is controlled through Azure RBAC.
words.longDefinition: Azure Container Registry (ACR) is a fully managed, private OCI-compliant registry for container images, Helm charts, and other OCI artifacts. It integrates with Azure Active Directory (Entra ID) for authentication via managed identity or service principal, and with Microsoft Defender for Containers for image vulnerability scanning. Geo-replication (on Premium tier) pushes images to multiple Azure regions so pulls are fast and resilient. ACR Tasks enables cloud-based image builds triggered by code commits or base-image updates, replacing the need for a separate CI build agent for container images. The registry integrates seamlessly with ACI, AKS, and Container Apps, which can pull using managed identity without credentials in code.
words.connector: Like a secure, private art vault: only credentialed curators can contribute, authenticated visitors can retrieve pieces, and copies exist in multiple cities.
words.techContext: Our CI pipeline pushes a signed image to Azure Container Registry after tests pass, and AKS pulls it using a managed identity.
words.exampleSentence: Enabling geo-replication on Azure Container Registry cut image pull times in the Southeast Asia region by 60%.

codeExample.code:
az acr create \
  --name myregistry --resource-group myRG \
  --sku Premium
az acr build \
  --registry myregistry --image api:latest .

words.etymology: From 'container' (Docker-style image) + 'registry' (a catalog/store); ACR launched in 2016.

words.shortDefinition: A serverless compute service that executes event-triggered code snippets and scales to zero between invocations.
words.simpleDefinition: You write a handler, choose a trigger (HTTP, timer, queue message, blob upload, event), and Azure runs it on demand with no servers to manage. Consumption plan instances appear in milliseconds and bill per execution. Durable Functions add stateful orchestrations on top.
words.longDefinition: Azure Functions is a fully managed, event-driven serverless compute platform where code is organized into functions — small units with a single trigger and optional input/output bindings. Triggers include HTTP, Timer, Azure Service Bus, Event Hub, Blob Storage, Cosmos DB change feed, and more; bindings declaratively connect to services without SDK boilerplate. The Consumption plan charges per execution and gigabyte-second and scales automatically from zero, while Premium and Dedicated (App Service) plans offer pre-warmed instances and VNet integration for lower cold-start sensitivity. The Durable Functions extension adds stateful orchestration patterns (fan-out/fan-in, async human approval, chaining) using checkpointed state stored in Azure Storage. Functions supports .NET, Node.js, Python, Java, PowerShell, and custom handlers.
words.connector: Like a light switch for compute: current only flows when you flip it, the wiring is already in place, and you pay only for the electricity used.
words.techContext: An HTTP-triggered Azure Functions endpoint validates webhook payloads and enqueues them for downstream processing within 200 ms.
words.exampleSentence: We replaced a polling daemon with an event-triggered handler in Azure Functions and eliminated the idle VM that ran it 24/7.

codeExample.code:
az functionapp create \
  --name myFuncApp --resource-group myRG \
  --storage-account mystorage \
  --consumption-plan-location eastus \
  --runtime python --runtime-version 3.11

words.etymology: From 'function' (a discrete unit of code); the Azure service launched in 2016 as the Azure counterpart to AWS Lambda.

words.shortDefinition: A low-code platform for automating multi-step workflows that connect hundreds of services through pre-built connectors.
words.simpleDefinition: You design workflows visually by chaining triggers and actions from a connector library (Office 365, Salesforce, SAP, Twitter, databases). The platform handles execution, retries, and state. It suits integration scenarios — syncing data, routing approvals, orchestrating business processes — without writing infrastructure code.
words.longDefinition: Azure Logic Apps is a cloud-native integration platform-as-a-service (iPaaS) for automating workflows and business processes. Workflows are defined declaratively (JSON-based, with a visual designer) and consist of a trigger and one or more actions drawn from hundreds of managed connectors covering SaaS, databases, storage, messaging, and custom APIs. The Standard tier (single-tenant, VNet injectable) suits enterprise workloads requiring isolation and private connectivity; the Consumption tier (multi-tenant) offers per-execution pricing. Connectors handle authentication, retrying, and pagination, and built-in control flow covers branching, looping, and error handling. Logic Apps integrates with Azure API Management, Service Bus, Event Grid, and Functions, often serving as the orchestration layer in event-driven and B2B integration architectures. It shares tooling with Power Automate at a lower-code end.
words.connector: Like a visual recipe card for a kitchen robot: drag-drop each step (stir, bake, plate), the robot executes it automatically, and adapters handle each appliance's quirks.
words.techContext: An Azure Logic Apps workflow listens on a SharePoint trigger, transforms the uploaded invoice with a connector, and posts the result to our ERP via SAP adapter.
words.exampleSentence: Finance replaced a brittle SFTP script with an Azure Logic Apps workflow that picks up files, converts formats, and updates the ledger automatically.

codeExample.code:
az logic workflow create \
  --resource-group myRG --name invoice-workflow \
  --definition @workflow-definition.json \
  --location eastus

words.etymology: From 'logic' (programmatic decision flow) + 'apps' (applications); launched as Azure Logic Apps in 2015.

words.shortDefinition: A managed pub/sub routing backbone that matches source notifications to handlers using declarative filter subscriptions.
words.simpleDefinition: It receives events from Azure services or your own code and routes them to subscribers (webhooks, Functions, Service Bus, Event Hubs) based on filter rules — no polling required. It delivers at-least-once and retries with exponential back-off. You pay per million events routed.
words.longDefinition: Azure Event Grid is a fully managed, serverless event-routing service based on a publish-subscribe model. Publishers include Azure services (Blob Storage, Resource Manager, Cognitive Services, IoT Hub) and custom applications posting to Event Grid topics or domains. Subscribers create event subscriptions with optional subject and event-type filters; matched events are delivered to handlers such as Azure Functions, Logic Apps, Service Bus queues, Event Hubs, or any HTTPS endpoint. Event Grid guarantees at-least-once delivery, applies exponential back-off retries for up to 24 hours, and supports dead-lettering to a Blob Storage container. It decouples producers from consumers, enables reactive architectures, and is the preferred mechanism for reacting to Azure resource lifecycle events (e.g., triggering a pipeline when a blob lands).
words.connector: Like a smart switchboard: each caller (publisher) dials in with a labelled message, and the board forwards it only to the extensions (subscribers) that opted in for that label.
words.techContext: A blob-created event from Azure Event Grid triggers our image-processing Azure Functions within milliseconds of upload, replacing a five-minute polling loop.
words.exampleSentence: We wired Azure Event Grid to forward every new Cosmos DB change to our audit logging function with two lines of subscription config.

codeExample.code:
az eventgrid event-subscription create \
  --name blob-to-func \
  --source-resource-id /subscriptions/SUB/resourceGroups/myRG/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/mystorage \
  --endpoint https://myfuncapp.azurewebsites.net/api/process

words.etymology: From 'event' (a discrete occurrence) + 'grid' (a network for distribution); Azure service launched in 2017.

words.shortDefinition: An enterprise-grade message broker supporting durable queues and topic-based publish/subscribe for reliable async communication.
words.simpleDefinition: It guarantees message delivery between producers and consumers with features like FIFO ordering, duplicate detection, sessions, and dead-letter queues. Topics with subscriptions let one message fan out to multiple independent consumers. It is the right choice when you need delivery guarantees, not just routing.
words.longDefinition: Azure Service Bus is a fully managed enterprise message broker that supports two messaging patterns: queues (point-to-point, competing consumers) and topics with subscriptions (publish/subscribe fan-out). Messages are durably stored and survive crashes; the broker guarantees at-least-once delivery, optionally exactly-once via deduplication. Advanced features include message sessions for FIFO processing per entity, scheduled delivery, time-to-live, dead-letter sub-queues, deferred processing, and auto-forwarding between entities. The Premium tier adds dedicated capacity, VNet service endpoints, and large message support (up to 100 MB). Service Bus is favored for transaction-style workflows, ordered processing, and workloads needing rich messaging semantics — complementing Event Grid (pure event routing) and Storage queues (simple durable buffering).
words.connector: Like a registered mail depot with sorting bins: letters arrive, are held safely, sorted by recipient, and handed over only when the recipient signs for them.
words.techContext: Each order flows through an Azure Service Bus topic with subscriptions routing to billing, inventory, and notification consumers independently.
words.exampleSentence: We moved checkout to Azure Service Bus queues after a downstream service outage caused silent message loss with our previous HTTP calls.

codeExample.code:
az servicebus namespace create \
  --name mysbns --resource-group myRG --sku Standard
az servicebus queue create \
  --namespace-name mysbns --resource-group myRG --name orders

words.etymology: Named after the 'bus' topology in computer architecture (a shared communication line) adapted for enterprise messaging.

words.shortDefinition: A Layer-4 (TCP/UDP) traffic distributor that spreads inbound flows across backend virtual machines within a region.
words.simpleDefinition: It operates at the transport layer, distributing connections across a backend pool of VMs using hash-based or session-affinity rules. It is highly available and zone-redundant, with health probes detecting unhealthy instances. There is no TLS inspection or URL routing — for that you need Application Gateway.
words.longDefinition: Azure Load Balancer is a fully managed, regional Layer-4 (TCP/UDP) load-balancing service. An external (public) load balancer distributes internet-facing traffic; an internal load balancer distributes traffic within a VNet. Rules map a front-end IP and port to a back-end pool of VM NICs or VMSS instances using a 5-tuple hash (source/dest IP, port, protocol) for distribution, with optional session persistence. Health probes (TCP, HTTP, HTTPS) remove unhealthy instances automatically. Standard SKU supports zone redundancy, SNAT for outbound flows, a global tier for cross-region distribution, and HA ports for NVA appliances. It handles tens of millions of flows with sub-millisecond forwarding and no SSL offload, keeping it simple, fast, and transparent to protocols above TCP.
words.connector: Like a traffic roundabout directing vehicles into equal lanes: it disperses the flow evenly without reading the passengers' destinations.
words.techContext: The Azure Load Balancer distributes TCP connections across three backend VMs and marks any that fail the health probe as out of rotation within 15 seconds.
words.exampleSentence: Adding a second VM to the Azure Load Balancer backend pool doubled our throughput without a single code change.

codeExample.code:
az network lb create \
  --name myLB --resource-group myRG \
  --sku Standard --public-ip-address myPIP \
  --backend-pool-name backendPool

words.etymology: Descriptive: a service that 'balances' network 'load' across servers; the Azure service has been available since 2012.

words.shortDefinition: A regional Layer-7 delivery controller with URL-based routing, TLS termination, session affinity, and a built-in web traffic firewall.
words.simpleDefinition: It understands HTTP/S and routes requests based on URL path or hostname to different backend pools, making it ideal for multi-service or microservice backends. It terminates TLS, rewrites headers, and optionally inspects and blocks malicious requests via its built-in WAF. It works within a single Azure region.
words.longDefinition: Azure Application Gateway is a fully managed Layer-7 (HTTP/HTTPS/HTTP2/WebSocket) application delivery controller. Listeners accept traffic on IP/port/hostname; request-routing rules send requests to backend pools (VMs, VMSS, App Service, AKS pods, IP addresses) based on path-based or multi-site routing. It terminates TLS (offloading decryption from backends), rewrites HTTP headers and URLs, enforces cookie-based session affinity, and integrates with Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) for OWASP protection. Auto-scaling (v2 SKU) adjusts capacity in under a minute based on traffic. Zone redundancy and private-frontend configurations support high-availability and internal use cases. It complements Azure Load Balancer (L4) and Azure Front Door (global L7) in the Azure traffic-management hierarchy.
words.connector: Like a smart maître d' who reads each reservation's details and directs guests to the right dining room, checks dress code at the door, and handles all coat-check logistics.
words.techContext: Application Gateway routes requests with /api/* to the AKS backend pool and /* to the static-site origin, all behind a WAF policy.
words.exampleSentence: Enabling the OWASP Core Rule Set on Application Gateway's WAF blocked the SQL injection attempts without touching the app code.

codeExample.code:
az network application-gateway create \
  --name myAppGW --resource-group myRG \
  --sku WAF_v2 --capacity 2 \
  --public-ip-address myPIP --vnet-name myVNet --subnet gwSubnet

words.etymology: From 'application' (Layer-7 awareness) + 'gateway' (a controlled network entry point); introduced by Azure in 2015.

words.shortDefinition: A global anycast edge service for HTTP/S load balancing, acceleration, and WAF protection across Azure regions.
words.simpleDefinition: It terminates connections at the nearest Microsoft edge PoP, accelerates traffic over the private Microsoft backbone to the closest healthy backend, and applies WAF rules at the edge. Unlike Application Gateway it is global — backends can be in multiple regions and failover is automatic. It also caches static content at the edge.
words.longDefinition: Azure Front Door (Standard/Premium) is a globally distributed, anycast Layer-7 service that combines CDN, global load balancing, origin health monitoring, WAF, and acceleration. Client requests terminate at the nearest of Microsoft's 200+ edge locations, and traffic travels over the Microsoft global WAN to the best healthy origin (Azure or non-Azure), minimizing public internet hops and improving latency and reliability. Traffic routing methods include latency-based, weighted, session-affinity, and geographic. The integrated WAF applies managed rule sets and custom rules at the edge before traffic reaches origins. Private Link integration (Premium) allows origins inside a VNet without public IPs. It replaces the legacy Azure Front Door Classic and consolidates Azure CDN, Traffic Manager, and Application Gateway for global-delivery architectures.
words.connector: Like an airline's hub with gates at every major city: passengers board at the nearest airport, the airline routes them privately to the destination city via the fastest internal path.
words.techContext: Azure Front Door routes North American users to the East US origin and European users to West Europe, failing over automatically if either goes unhealthy.
words.exampleSentence: Adding Azure Front Door in front of our multi-region app cut median latency for Asian users by 40% and gave us instant failover.

codeExample.code:
az afd profile create \
  --profile-name myFrontDoor \
  --resource-group myRG \
  --sku Premium_AzureFrontDoor

words.etymology: Front Door evokes the primary entry point to a building; 'Azure Front Door' positions it as the global front of Azure-hosted services.

words.shortDefinition: A managed, cloud-native stateful network security service that controls and logs traffic crossing a virtual network perimeter.
words.simpleDefinition: It is a fully stateful, managed service deployed in a hub VNet to inspect and filter all inbound, outbound, and east-west traffic with application FQDN rules, network rules, NAT rules, and threat intelligence. You do not patch or manage VMs — Azure operates the underlying infrastructure. Premium adds TLS inspection and IDPS.
words.longDefinition: Azure Firewall is a cloud-native, stateful layer-3 to layer-7 network security service that provides centralized traffic control for Azure Virtual Networks. It is deployed in a dedicated subnet and scales automatically. Rule collection types include DNAT (inbound port forwarding), network (IP/port/protocol), and application (FQDN-based HTTP/S) rules, processed in priority order. Built-in threat intelligence (Microsoft Threat Intel feed) can deny or alert on known-malicious IPs and domains. The Premium SKU adds TLS inspection (break-and-inspect), an IDPS (intrusion detection and prevention system) with signature-based rules, and URL filtering. Azure Firewall Policy provides a hierarchical policy model for organization-wide rulesets. It integrates with Azure Monitor, Sentinel, and Virtual WAN for centralized security and logging in hub-and-spoke and Virtual WAN topologies.
words.connector: Like a staffed security gatehouse at the entrance to an industrial estate: every vehicle's papers are checked against a rulebook before it is waved through or turned away.
words.techContext: All internet-destined traffic from spoke VNets routes through Azure Firewall in the hub, where application rules permit only approved FQDNs.
words.exampleSentence: Enabling threat intelligence on Azure Firewall automatically blocked traffic to a known command-and-control domain before we even saw the alert.

codeExample.code:
az network firewall create \
  --name myFirewall --resource-group myRG \
  --location eastus
az network firewall policy create \
  --name myFWPolicy --resource-group myRG

words.etymology: From 'firewall' (a barrier preventing fire spread), repurposed in computing for network traffic barriers; the Azure service launched in 2018.

words.shortDefinition: A managed Azure service that establishes encrypted IPsec/IKE tunnels between a virtual network and on-premises or remote networks.
words.simpleDefinition: It creates an encrypted tunnel over the public internet that makes your on-premises data center or remote devices appear as if they are directly attached to your Azure VNet. Site-to-site connects entire networks; point-to-site connects individual devices. It is slower and cheaper than ExpressRoute.
words.longDefinition: Azure VPN Gateway is a managed, zone-redundant gateway service deployed into a VNet's GatewaySubnet that enables cross-premises connectivity via IPsec/IKE encrypted tunnels. Site-to-site (S2S) connections link on-premises VPN devices to Azure over the internet; point-to-site (P2S) allows individual clients to connect using OpenVPN, SSTP, or IKEv2. VNet-to-VNet connections link two Azure VNets in the same or different regions. Gateway SKUs from Basic to VpnGw5AZ determine aggregate throughput (100 Mbps–100 Gbps), tunnel count, and BGP/zone-redundancy support. BGP-enabled gateways dynamically exchange routes with on-premises routers. Active-active mode with two public IPs provides gateway-level redundancy. It is the standard path for hybrid connectivity when dedicated fiber is not justified or as encrypted backup alongside ExpressRoute.
words.connector: Like a secure postal tube between your office and the data center: parcels travel through public infrastructure but are sealed in encryption so no one can tamper with them.
words.techContext: The branch office connects to the Azure VNet over a VPN Gateway site-to-site tunnel, giving developers direct access to dev resources.
words.exampleSentence: We provisioned a VPN Gateway in under an hour to establish the pilot hybrid connection before ExpressRoute provisioning completed.

codeExample.code:
az network vnet-gateway create \
  --name myVpnGW --resource-group myRG \
  --vnet myVNet --public-ip-address myPIP \
  --gateway-type Vpn --sku VpnGw2AZ

words.etymology: 'VPN' = Virtual Private Network (1990s networking term); 'gateway' denotes the managed network border device.

words.shortDefinition: A private, dedicated fiber circuit between an on-premises location and Azure, bypassing the public internet entirely.
words.simpleDefinition: A connectivity provider or co-location facility gives you a physical or virtual cross-connect into Microsoft's edge; your traffic never traverses the internet. It offers consistent bandwidth from 50 Mbps to 100 Gbps and lower, more predictable latency than VPN. Provisioning takes weeks because real cabling is involved.
words.longDefinition: Azure ExpressRoute establishes a dedicated private circuit between an organization's premises or co-location facility and Microsoft's network edge through an authorized connectivity provider. Traffic travels over the provider's network or a direct cross-connect, never the public internet, delivering consistent bandwidth, low jitter, and throughput up to 100 Gbps (ExpressRoute Direct). Virtual circuits (ExpressRoute circuits) multiplex into private peering (to Azure VNets via an ExpressRoute Gateway), Microsoft peering (to Azure public services like Storage and O365), and optionally Global Reach (connecting two on-premises sites through Microsoft). Circuits offer 99.95% SLA with two active border connections by default. ExpressRoute suits large, steady data movement, latency-sensitive applications, and compliance requirements mandating private connectivity, often with a VPN Gateway as encrypted backup.
words.connector: Like leasing a reserved private lane on a highway, separate from public traffic: dedicated bandwidth, guaranteed speed, and nobody else sharing your asphalt.
words.techContext: The production database replication crosses into Azure over ExpressRoute, meeting the compliance requirement for data never touching the public internet.
words.exampleSentence: After switching from site-to-site VPN to ExpressRoute, database round-trip latency dropped from 18 ms to 4 ms.

codeExample.code:
az network express-route create \
  --name myCircuit --resource-group myRG \
  --peering-location "Silicon Valley" \
  --bandwidth 1000 --provider "Equinix" --sku-tier Standard

words.etymology: From 'express' (fast, direct) + 'route' (a network path); the Azure service launched in 2014.

words.shortDefinition: A hosting service for DNS zones that uses Microsoft's global anycast infrastructure to answer domain queries reliably and quickly.
words.simpleDefinition: You delegate your domain to Azure's name servers and manage records (A, CNAME, MX, TXT) via the Azure portal, CLI, or API. It supports public zones for internet-facing names and private zones for VNet-internal resolution. Alias records keep Azure-resource DNS entries in sync automatically.
words.longDefinition: Azure DNS hosts DNS zones on Microsoft's globally distributed anycast name-server infrastructure, providing low-latency, highly available resolution backed by a 100% availability SLA. Public zones serve internet-facing DNS; private zones are linked to VNets for internal name resolution without custom DNS servers. Alias record sets point to Azure resources (public IP, Traffic Manager, Front Door, CDN) and update automatically when the resource's IP changes, eliminating stale A records. Role-based access control (RBAC) governs who can create or modify records, and Azure Monitor diagnostics capture query logs. Azure DNS does not currently offer domain registration — you register domains with registrars and delegate NS records to Azure's name servers. It integrates with Private Endpoint for resolving private-link FQDNs within VNets.
words.connector: Like running a phone directory inside Microsoft's global post office network: every lookup is answered at the closest branch instantly, and your address book is editable from one admin console.
words.techContext: We created a private Azure DNS zone for our VNet so Cosmos DB private endpoints resolve by friendly name inside the network.
words.exampleSentence: Switching our public zone to Azure DNS and using an alias record to Front Door meant we never had to update the A record manually again.

codeExample.code:
az network dns zone create \
  --resource-group myRG --name contoso.com
az network dns record-set a add-record \
  --resource-group myRG --zone-name contoso.com \
  --record-set-name @ --ipv4-address 203.0.113.10

words.etymology: DNS = Domain Name System (1983 internet standard); 'Azure DNS' simply denotes Microsoft's managed hosting of DNS zones.

words.shortDefinition: A fully managed cloud-based file share accessible over the SMB or NFS protocol, mountable on Windows, Linux, and macOS.
words.simpleDefinition: It provides persistent, shared file storage that multiple VMs or on-premises machines can mount simultaneously just like a traditional network drive. There is no file server to patch or manage. It supports snapshotting, Azure File Sync to cache shares on-premises, and identity-based access control.
words.longDefinition: Azure Files delivers fully managed file shares in the cloud accessible via SMB 2.1/3.x and NFS 4.1 protocols, as well as the REST API. Shares are backed by Azure Storage accounts and scale to 100 TiB per share on standard (HDD) or premium (SSD) tiers. Multiple clients — cloud VMs, on-premises servers, or developer machines — can mount the same share concurrently with standard mount commands, making it a drop-in replacement for on-premises file servers and a natural lift-and-shift target for legacy NAS workloads. Azure File Sync replicates shares to Windows Server caches for low-latency on-premises access with cloud-tiering to reclaim local disk. Snapshots capture point-in-time read-only copies; share-level SMB ACLs integrate with Active Directory for identity-based permissions. It is the recommended choice for persistent shared storage in container and VM workloads.
words.connector: Like a USB drive floating in the cloud: plug it into any machine with the right credentials, drag and drop files, and everyone else sees the changes immediately.
words.techContext: Legacy app servers that expected a UNC path were re-pointed to an Azure Files SMB share during migration, with zero code changes.
words.exampleSentence: We replaced a self-managed Windows file server with Azure Files and let Azure File Sync keep the on-site cache warm for the remote office.

codeExample.code:
az storage share-rm create \
  --resource-group myRG --storage-account mystorage \
  --name myshare --quota 1024
# Mount on Linux: mount -t cifs //mystorage.file.core.windows.net/myshare /mnt/myshare

words.etymology: Descriptive: 'Azure Files' = Azure-hosted file storage; the service launched in 2015.

words.shortDefinition: A globally distributed, multi-model NoSQL database with guaranteed single-digit-millisecond latency and configurable consistency levels.
words.simpleDefinition: You choose a data model API (NoSQL/document, MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin graph, or Table) and Cosmos DB handles replication to any Azure region you select. Writes and reads can be served locally with tunable consistency from strong to eventual. It scales throughput independently of storage.
words.longDefinition: Azure Cosmos DB is a globally distributed, multi-model database service that decouples compute (Request Units, RU/s) from storage and replicates data to any number of Azure regions with configurable consistency (strong, bounded-staleness, session, consistent-prefix, eventual). APIs include NoSQL (document JSON, native API), MongoDB (wire-compatible), Cassandra (CQL), Gremlin (graph traversal), and Azure Table Storage (key-value). Point reads and writes are served from the local region with sub-10 ms latency at the 99th percentile. Multi-region writes (active-active) enable low-latency global writes, using a last-writer-wins or custom conflict resolution policy. Serverless mode bills per RU consumed without provisioning throughput. The change feed (a persistent, ordered log of item changes) enables event-driven processing and replication.
words.connector: Like a global franchise restaurant that has the same menu everywhere, serves customers from the nearest kitchen, and syncs the recipe book across all locations automatically.
words.techContext: User profiles are stored in Azure Cosmos DB, replicated to four regions with session consistency, so reads and writes are always local.
words.exampleSentence: After turning on multi-region writes in Azure Cosmos DB, API latency in Australia dropped from 120 ms to 8 ms.

codeExample.code:
az cosmosdb create \
  --name mycosmosdb --resource-group myRG \
  --locations regionName=eastus failoverPriority=0 \
  --locations regionName=westeurope failoverPriority=1

words.etymology: From 'cosmos' (the universe, evoking global scale); the service was originally called DocumentDB before rebranding in 2017.

words.shortDefinition: A managed in-memory data store that serves sub-millisecond key-value lookups for caching, session state, and pub/sub messaging.
words.simpleDefinition: It runs a fully managed Redis instance so you can cache database results, share session state between app servers, and implement simple queues or pub/sub without managing Redis infrastructure. Tiers range from Basic (single node) to Premium (clustering, persistence, VNet injection) to Enterprise (Redis Stack).
words.longDefinition: Azure Cache for Redis is a fully managed Redis service that provides in-memory, key-value storage with sub-millisecond response times. It supports all standard Redis data structures (strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, bitmaps, HyperLogLog, streams) and commands. The Basic and Standard tiers offer single-node or replicated caches with automatic failover; Premium adds clustering (horizontal sharding), Redis persistence (RDB/AOF) for durability, private VNet injection, and geo-replication for cross-region read replicas; Enterprise and Enterprise Flash tiers provide Redis Stack (RedisSearch, RedisJSON, RedisTimeSeries) on dedicated hardware, including SSD-backed capacity. Common use cases include read-aside caching for relational databases, distributed session state in stateless web apps, rate limiting, and lightweight messaging via Redis Pub/Sub or Streams.
words.connector: Like a sticky note pad on the desk: the most-used information lives in arm's reach for instant lookup, freeing the filing cabinet (database) for less-frequent deep retrievals.
words.techContext: Product detail pages load in under 50 ms because Azure Cache for Redis serves the serialized JSON, sparing the SQL database from repetitive catalog queries.
words.exampleSentence: Moving session storage to Azure Cache for Redis let us remove sticky-session affinity on the load balancer and deploy additional instances freely.

codeExample.code:
az redis create \
  --name myredis --resource-group myRG \
  --location eastus --sku Premium \
  --vm-size P1

words.etymology: Redis = REmote DIctionary Server (open-source project by Salvatore Sanfilippo, 2009); 'Azure Cache for Redis' denotes Microsoft's managed hosting.

words.shortDefinition: A managed HSM-backed store for secrets, encryption keys, and TLS certificates with RBAC and audit-logged access.
words.simpleDefinition: Applications retrieve database passwords, API keys, and certificates from Key Vault at runtime via managed identity rather than hardcoding them. The service stores sensitive material in FIPS 140-2 validated hardware (Standard or HSM tiers), logs every access, and handles certificate lifecycle. It eliminates secrets from code and config files.
words.longDefinition: Azure Key Vault provides secure, centralized management of secrets (arbitrary text values like connection strings), cryptographic keys (RSA and EC keys for encrypt/sign operations), and X.509 certificates including automated renewal via configured certificate authorities. Access is governed by Azure RBAC with fine-grained Key Vault-level or object-level permissions (secrets officer, crypto user, reader, etc.) and optionally enhanced with access policies. All operations are logged to Azure Monitor and can be streamed to a Log Analytics workspace or SIEM. The Standard tier uses software protection; the Premium tier uses an FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated HSM. Managed HSM is a single-tenant, dedicated HSM service for highest-assurance key material. Soft-delete and purge protection prevent accidental or malicious permanent deletion. Applications authenticate using managed identity — no stored credential needed.
words.connector: Like a bank safe deposit box for digital valuables: the bank (Azure) manages the vault and keeps the access ledger, and each authorized account holder shows their ID to retrieve their items.
words.techContext: The app's managed identity is granted 'Key Vault Secrets User' and retrieves the database connection string from Azure Key Vault on startup.
words.exampleSentence: After the credential-leak postmortem, we stored all secrets in Azure Key Vault so no app config file or environment variable ever holds a plaintext password.

codeExample.code:
az keyvault create \
  --name myKV --resource-group myRG \
  --enable-rbac-authorization true
az keyvault secret set \
  --vault-name myKV --name dbPassword --value 's3cr3t'

words.etymology: From 'key' (cryptographic key) + 'vault' (a secure strongroom); the Azure service launched in 2015.

words.shortDefinition: An automatically provisioned Entra ID principal tied to an Azure resource, used to authenticate to other services without stored credentials.
words.simpleDefinition: When you enable a managed identity on a VM, function, or container, Azure creates and rotates the credential automatically. The resource can then authenticate to Key Vault, Storage, or Cosmos DB using that identity and role assignments — no passwords, connection strings, or certificates in code. There is a system-assigned form (1:1 with resource lifecycle) and user-assigned (shareable).
words.longDefinition: A managed identity is an Entra ID (Azure Active Directory) service principal whose credential lifecycle is entirely managed by the Azure platform — creation, rotation, and deletion happen automatically with no developer involvement. System-assigned identities are bound to a single resource and deleted when the resource is deleted; user-assigned identities are standalone resources that can be attached to multiple resources simultaneously, enabling credential sharing across a fleet. Code running on an enabled resource obtains an access token by calling the Azure Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) endpoint, passing the target resource URI, with no secrets ever stored in code, config, or environment variables. Role assignments on target resources grant the identity the minimum necessary permissions. Managed identity is the recommended authentication mechanism for all Azure-to-Azure service access, replacing service principals with manually managed secrets.
words.connector: Like an employee badge that the HR department issues, rotates, and revokes automatically: you show your badge at each door and it is always valid without you ever managing the key.
words.techContext: The Azure Functions app uses a system-assigned managed identity to pull secrets from Key Vault, so there are no credentials in any deployment artifact.
words.exampleSentence: We eliminated the last hardcoded connection string by assigning a managed identity to the container app and granting it 'Storage Blob Data Reader' on the account.

codeExample.code:
# Enable system-assigned identity on a VM and assign a role
az vm identity assign --name myVM --resource-group myRG
az role assignment create \
  --role "Key Vault Secrets User" \
  --assignee-object-id $(az vm identity show --name myVM --resource-group myRG --query principalId -o tsv) \
  --scope /subscriptions/SUB/resourceGroups/myRG/providers/Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/myKV

words.etymology: From 'managed' (administered by the platform) + 'identity' (an Entra ID principal); the feature launched as 'Managed Service Identity' in 2017 and was renamed.

words.shortDefinition: The unified observability platform that collects, correlates, and acts on metrics, logs, and traces from across Azure and on-premises.
words.simpleDefinition: It is the single pane for all monitoring data in Azure: resource metrics flow in automatically, diagnostic logs are routed to Log Analytics or a storage account, and alert rules fire actions when thresholds are breached. Dashboards, workbooks, and integrations with Grafana surface insights. Everything else — Application Insights, Log Analytics, Container Insights — is built on top of it.
words.longDefinition: Azure Monitor is the overarching platform service that ingests, stores, and acts on telemetry from Azure resources, on-premises infrastructure, and applications. It collects platform metrics (free, 93-day retention, 1-minute granularity) automatically from every Azure resource and routes diagnostic logs, activity logs, and custom metrics to destinations such as Log Analytics workspaces, Azure Storage, Event Hubs, or partner integrations. Alert rules evaluate conditions on metrics or log queries (KQL) and trigger action groups (email, SMS, webhook, runbook, ITSM). Diagnostic settings, data collection rules, and the Azure Monitor Agent provide flexible collection pipelines. Visualization tools include Azure Dashboards, Metrics Explorer, Workbooks, and native Grafana data-source integration. Child services — Application Insights (APM), Container Insights (AKS), Network Insights, and VM Insights — all store their data in Log Analytics workspaces and surface curated views on top of the same platform.
words.connector: Like a hospital's central monitoring station: every room's vitals feed into one console, alarms trigger when readings go out of range, and the full history is on file for any patient.
words.techContext: We centralized all Azure Monitor diagnostic settings to a shared Log Analytics workspace so security, ops, and dev query the same data with KQL.
words.exampleSentence: An Azure Monitor alert on the p99 HTTP latency metric paged the on-call engineer before any customers reported errors.

codeExample.code:
az monitor metrics alert create \
  --name high-cpu --resource-group myRG \
  --scopes /subscriptions/SUB/resourceGroups/myRG/providers/Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/myVM \
  --condition "avg Percentage CPU > 85" --window-size 5m

words.etymology: Descriptive name: a service that 'monitors' resources on Azure; the consolidated Azure Monitor brand was introduced in 2018.

words.shortDefinition: A workspace service that stores log and metric data and lets you query it with the Kusto Query Language for analysis and alerting.
words.simpleDefinition: Log Analytics workspaces are the central repository where Azure Monitor stores diagnostic logs, security events, and telemetry. You query the data using KQL, set up dashboards and alert rules on query results, and integrate with Sentinel for SIEM. Almost every Azure observability feature routes its data here.
words.longDefinition: Log Analytics is the Azure Monitor component that provides a managed data platform for collecting, indexing, and querying log and performance data using Kusto Query Language (KQL). A Log Analytics workspace is the top-level boundary — resources send diagnostic logs via diagnostic settings or data collection rules, and solutions (Container Insights, VM Insights, Application Insights) write their data here. KQL allows powerful time-series analysis, joins across tables, aggregations, and machine-learning functions (anomaly detection, clustering). Workspaces offer configurable data retention (30 days–7 years), data export to Storage or Event Hubs, cross-workspace querying, and row-level security through table-level RBAC. Microsoft Sentinel is built on Log Analytics and consumes workspace data for threat detection. The workspace model decouples storage from compute, enabling any number of services to query the same data without data-movement overhead.
words.connector: Like a building's centralized system log room: every elevator, HVAC unit, and security camera sends its records here, and investigators query them all in one place.
words.techContext: Our security team runs hourly KQL queries against the Log Analytics workspace to detect failed authentication bursts across all subscriptions.
words.exampleSentence: Writing a five-line KQL query in Log Analytics uncovered which Azure Functions app was generating 80% of the error log volume.

codeExample.code:
// Top 5 error sources in the last hour
AppExceptions
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| summarize ErrorCount = count() by AppRoleName
| top 5 by ErrorCount desc

words.etymology: From 'log' (a recorded event) + 'analytics' (systematic analysis); integrated into Azure Monitor in 2018.

words.shortDefinition: A performance monitoring service that traces requests, dependencies, exceptions, and user journeys across distributed apps.
words.simpleDefinition: You add the Application Insights SDK or enable auto-instrumentation on App Service or Azure Functions, and it captures every request, dependency call, exception, and custom event. A distributed trace map shows how requests flow across microservices. It also tracks user behavior and page performance in browsers.
words.longDefinition: Application Insights is the APM (Application Performance Monitoring) service within Azure Monitor, storing all data in a Log Analytics workspace. It captures server-side request telemetry (rate, duration, failure rate), dependency tracking (HTTP, SQL, Redis calls with timing), exceptions with stack traces, custom events and metrics, and distributed traces correlating across services via a W3C TraceContext or AI correlation header. The Application Map visualizes service topology and latency/error rates per dependency. Availability tests (ping, multi-step) run synthetic transactions from global locations. Live Metrics Stream provides sub-second real-time dashboards. Smart Detection (Adaptive Anomaly Detection) alerts on unusual changes in failure rates or latency without manual threshold configuration. SDKs are available for .NET, Java, Node.js, Python, and JavaScript (browser); OpenTelemetry-based auto-instrumentation is the recommended modern approach.
words.connector: Like a flight data recorder for your app: every request, every dependency call, and every error is captured in sequence so you can reconstruct exactly what happened on any flight.
words.techContext: Application Insights end-to-end transaction search showed the downstream Redis timeout that caused 5% of checkout requests to fail.
words.exampleSentence: Turning on Application Insights on the API immediately revealed that 20% of requests were spending 800 ms waiting on a slow SQL query we had never noticed.

codeExample.code:
az monitor app-insights component create \
  --app myAppInsights --resource-group myRG \
  --location eastus \
  --workspace /subscriptions/SUB/resourceGroups/myRG/providers/Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces/myLAW

words.etymology: From 'application' (the monitored software) + 'insights' (actionable understanding from data); launched as a preview in 2014.

words.shortDefinition: A group of identically configured, load-balanced VMs that expand and contract automatically based on demand or a schedule.
words.simpleDefinition: You define a VM template and a capacity range; Azure creates multiple identical VMs, attaches them to a load balancer, and adjusts count based on CPU, memory, or custom metrics. Failed instances are replaced automatically. It is the standard way to run stateless workloads that must handle variable load.
words.longDefinition: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets (VMSS) provision and manage a fleet of identically configured VMs (from 0 to thousands) as a single resource. All VMs share the same image, SKU, extensions, and network configuration, enabling consistent deployment at scale. The built-in autoscaler adjusts instance count based on host metrics (CPU, memory, inbound flows), guest metrics via Azure Monitor Agent, or custom metrics from App Insights or event queues using KEDA-style rules. Flexible orchestration mode (recommended) places VMs across fault and update domains spanning availability zones for high availability. Spot priority enables large-scale batch processing on spare capacity. Rolling upgrade policies update VMs in batches with health checks so no-downtime updates are possible. VMSS underpins Azure Kubernetes Service node pools, Service Fabric clusters, and Batch compute nodes internally.
words.connector: Like a photocopier that also shreds excess copies: it prints more VMs as the workload grows and destroys them automatically when demand drops, always keeping the queue moving.
words.techContext: The encoding service runs on a Virtual Machine Scale Set that scales from 2 to 40 GPU VMs based on a job-queue metric, then returns to 2 overnight.
words.exampleSentence: After migrating the stateless API tier to a Virtual Machine Scale Set, traffic spikes no longer caused errors — the fleet just added more instances.

codeExample.code:
az vmss create \
  --name myScaleSet --resource-group myRG \
  --image Ubuntu2204 --vm-sku Standard_D4s_v5 \
  --instance-count 2 --lb myLB

words.etymology: Descriptive: a 'set' of 'virtual machines' that 'scale'; the feature launched as VM Scale Sets in 2015.

words.shortDefinition: A managed PaaS service that provides secure, browser-based RDP and SSH access to VMs through the Azure portal without exposing public IPs.
words.simpleDefinition: You deploy Azure Bastion into a subnet and it proxies RDP and SSH sessions through the portal or the native client over TLS 443, so VMs need no public IPs and no inbound RDP/SSH ports in their NSG. Administrators connect in the browser with Azure Active Directory authentication and all sessions are logged. It is the recommended replacement for jump boxes.
words.longDefinition: Azure Bastion is a fully platform-managed PaaS service deployed into an AzureBastionSubnet (/26 or larger) within a VNet. It acts as a TLS-secured reverse proxy for RDP (Windows) and SSH (Linux) sessions: users authenticate via the Azure portal or native client using their Entra ID credentials, and the session is proxied over port 443 to the target VM's private IP, with no RDP/SSH port exposed to the internet and no public IP on the VM. The Standard SKU adds session recording, shareable links, IP-based connection, and support for VMs in peered VNets (without deploying Bastion in each). The Developer SKU (preview) is a fully shared, serverless tier with no AzureBastionSubnet required. All sessions appear in Azure Activity Log and can be streamed to Log Analytics. It replaces the traditional jump-box/bastion-host VM pattern with a managed, zero-footprint alternative.
words.connector: Like a secure lobby with a staffed reception desk: visitors authenticate at the front and are escorted directly to the right office without ever being given a key to the building's exterior.
words.techContext: After deploying Azure Bastion, we removed all public IPs and inbound RDP NSG rules from 200 VMs, shrinking the attack surface dramatically.
words.exampleSentence: The security audit found zero open RDP ports because every administrator connects through Azure Bastion instead.

codeExample.code:
az network bastion create \
  --name myBastion --resource-group myRG \
  --vnet-name myVNet --public-ip-address myBastionPIP \
  --sku Standard

words.etymology: From 'bastion' (a projecting fortification), the traditional security term for a hardened entry-point host.

words.shortDefinition: A centralized, cloud-native protection service that snapshots and retains VMs, disks, databases, and on-premises workloads with policy-driven schedules.
words.simpleDefinition: You configure backup policies that define frequency and retention, associate them with resources, and Azure Backup handles scheduling, storing backup data in a Recovery Services vault, and providing a restore workflow. It supports application-consistent snapshots for SQL Server and SAP HANA and cross-region restore for disaster recovery.
words.longDefinition: Azure Backup is a fully managed, scalable data-protection service built on Recovery Services vaults (and the newer Backup vaults). It supports Azure VMs (agent-based and agentless disk snapshots), Azure Managed Disks, Azure Files shares, Azure Blobs, SQL Server in VMs, SAP HANA in VMs, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, and on-premises resources via the MARS agent or Azure Backup Server. Backup policies control backup schedule, daily/weekly/monthly/yearly retention, and whether instant restore snapshots are kept for quick recovery. Storage is geo-redundant (GRS), locally redundant (LRS), or zone-redundant (ZRS). Soft-delete protects backup data for 14 additional days after deletion. Backup Center provides a centralized view across vaults and subscriptions. Cross-Region Restore allows restoring a VM to a secondary region from the paired geo-redundant vault replica.
words.connector: Like a professional archiving firm that collects copies of your files on a schedule, stores them in a secure offsite warehouse, and retrieves any version on demand.
words.techContext: Azure Backup policies set daily snapshots with 30-day retention for VMs and annual recovery points for the SQL databases, all monitored from Backup Center.
words.exampleSentence: When a developer accidentally deleted a production database, Azure Backup restored the SQL Server to the previous day's state in under 20 minutes.

codeExample.code:
az backup protection enable-for-vm \
  --resource-group myRG --vault-name myRSV \
  --vm myVM --policy-name DefaultPolicy

words.etymology: Descriptive: 'Azure Backup' — the Azure service for creating backup copies; launched in 2014.

words.shortDefinition: A billing commitment that exchanges a 1- or 3-year upfront or monthly payment for a significant discount on Azure compute or other service usage.
words.simpleDefinition: If you know a VM size will run continuously for at least a year, a Reserved Instance can cut the cost by up to 72% versus pay-as-you-go. The reservation is a billing construct, not a specific VM — it automatically applies to any matching running VM in your subscription. Savings can be exchanged or refunded (subject to limits).
words.longDefinition: Azure Reserved VM Instances (RIs) — part of the broader Azure Reservations portfolio — are 1-year or 3-year billing commitments for specific VM families, sizes, and regions that reduce the compute price by up to 72% compared to pay-as-you-go rates. A reservation is applied automatically by the billing system to matching running VMs in the same subscription or shared scope across an enrollment; no VM reconfiguration is required. Reserved Instances cover VMs, SQL Database, Cosmos DB, App Service, Azure Databricks, and other services. Flexibility options (instance size flexibility for VM families) allow the discount to apply across different sizes within the same family. Unused reservation hours are forfeited within a billing period, so they suit stable, predictable baseline workloads rather than variable ones. Self-service exchange and cancellation (with a small fee) provide flexibility if needs change.
words.connector: Like buying an annual public-transport pass instead of daily tickets: you commit for the year at a discounted rate and recoup the savings by riding every day.
words.techContext: We purchased Azure Reserved Instances for our database-tier VMs and cut the three-year TCO by 58% compared to the pay-as-you-go forecast.
words.exampleSentence: After right-sizing the VM fleet, finance bought Azure Reserved Instances for the stable baseline and left burst capacity on pay-as-you-go.

codeExample.code:
# View reservation utilization across subscriptions
az reservations reservation list \
  --reservation-order-id ORDER_ID \
  --query '[].{Name:name,State:properties.provisioningState}'

words.etymology: From 'reserved' (pre-committed capacity) + 'instances' (VM occurrences); modeled on AWS Reserved Instances; the Azure feature launched in 2017.

words.shortDefinition: Virtual machines that run on unused Azure capacity at steep discounts but can be evicted with 30-second notice when capacity is reclaimed.
words.simpleDefinition: Azure offers idle datacenter capacity at up to 90% discount as Spot VMs. The catch is that Azure can evict them with 30 seconds' warning whenever it needs the capacity back for regular customers. They are ideal for fault-tolerant batch jobs, rendering, or CI pipelines that can checkpoint and resume.
words.longDefinition: Azure Spot Virtual Machines allow tenants to bid for and use unused Azure compute capacity at prices that fluctuate with supply, offering savings of up to 90% versus pay-as-you-go. When Azure needs the capacity back for standard-priority customers, Spot VMs receive an eviction notice via the Azure Scheduled Events endpoint (30 seconds for VMs, 30 seconds for VMSS instances) before being stopped or deleted, depending on the eviction policy. Eviction can also be triggered if the spot price exceeds a user-defined max price. Because eviction can happen at any time, applications must be designed to checkpoint state, use queues for durable work items, or run stateless batch workloads. Spot VMs are available as standalone VMs or as Spot priority nodes in Virtual Machine Scale Sets, making them the basis for cost-efficient, large-scale batch and HPC. They cannot be used for SLA-sensitive or always-on production workloads.
words.connector: Like stand-by seats on a flight: dramatically cheaper than reserved seats but the airline can bump you if the flight fills up, so you pack light and stay ready to rebook.
words.techContext: The genomics pipeline runs nightly on Azure Spot VMs in a Scale Set, using Azure Storage Queue to re-queue any job whose VM was evicted.
words.exampleSentence: Switching the nightly model-training job to Azure Spot VMs cut the GPU bill by 78% with only occasional re-runs when eviction hit.

codeExample.code:
az vm create \
  --name spotWorker --resource-group myRG \
  --image Ubuntu2204 --size Standard_D8s_v5 \
  --priority Spot --eviction-policy Deallocate \
  --max-price 0.10

words.etymology: From 'spot' (the open-market spot price, a commodities trading term for immediate, variable-price purchases).

words.shortDefinition: A simple, durable, massively scalable first-in-first-out buffer for asynchronously decoupling producers from consumers.
words.simpleDefinition: Producers post text messages (up to 64 KB) to a queue URL; consumers poll and delete them after processing. Messages can be hidden temporarily while in-flight so others do not pick them up concurrently. It holds up to 500 TB and costs a fraction of a cent per million operations.
words.longDefinition: Azure Storage queues are part of Azure Storage accounts, providing a simple, RESTful message queue service for decoupling producers and consumers in distributed architectures. Messages are up to 64 KB of arbitrary text (commonly JSON or Base64-encoded binary), have configurable TTL (up to 7 days, or infinite), and support a visibility timeout so a consumer can lock a message while processing — preventing double-processing — and the message reappears if not deleted within the timeout. Queue depth is virtually unlimited (bounded by the 500 TB storage account limit) and throughput scales with the number of consumers polling concurrently. Integration with Azure Functions (queue trigger) enables serverless processing. It complements Azure Service Bus queues (which offer sessions, dead-lettering, transactions, and larger messages) for simpler, cost-sensitive, high-volume scenarios that do not need advanced messaging features.
words.connector: Like a ticket machine in a bakery: customers pull a numbered ticket (enqueue) and wait; staff serve the next number (dequeue) one at a time, never skipping ahead.
words.techContext: Resize jobs are enqueued to an Azure Storage queue; multiple Azure Functions workers poll the queue and scale out automatically based on queue depth.
words.exampleSentence: We decoupled the upload API from the processing pipeline using an Azure Storage queue so a spike in uploads no longer slows down conversion jobs.

codeExample.code:
az storage queue create \
  --account-name mystorage --name job-queue
az storage message put \
  --account-name mystorage --queue-name job-queue \
  --content '{"jobId":"123","file":"video.mp4"}'

words.etymology: From 'queue' (an ordered waiting line, from French 'queue' = tail); the Azure Storage Queue service has been available since 2009.

words.shortDefinition: A managed service that continuously replicates workloads to a secondary region and orchestrates failover and failback for business continuity.
words.simpleDefinition: It replicates Azure VMs (or on-premises Hyper-V/VMware workloads) to a secondary Azure region and keeps replication in sync. When disaster strikes, you trigger a failover that boots VMs in the secondary region from the latest replicated state. Recovery plans automate the sequence and allow test failovers without disruption.
words.longDefinition: Azure Site Recovery (ASR) provides business continuity by continuously replicating VMs and workloads to a recovery location and enabling orchestrated failover. For Azure-to-Azure scenarios, ASR replicates VMs using change-block tracking to a target region, achieving RPOs down to a few minutes and RTOs of about an hour. It supports on-premises VMware, Hyper-V, and physical servers replicating to Azure, with the Mobility Service agent capturing disk writes. Recovery plans define the failover order of multiple VMs, include pre- and post-failover scripts (Azure Automation runbooks), and allow test failover into an isolated VNet to verify DR readiness without impacting production. Failback returns VMs to the primary region after it recovers. ASR stores replication data in a cache storage account and logs replication health to Azure Monitor.
words.connector: Like a continuously updated shadow building for your factory: construction mirrors every change to the main site, so if the main building burns down you can open the shadow site within the hour.
words.techContext: Azure Site Recovery replicates the ERP tier to West Europe with 15-minute RPO, and the team tests failover quarterly using recovery plans with runbook automation.
words.exampleSentence: When the primary region experienced an extended outage, Azure Site Recovery let us fail over 30 VMs in under 45 minutes using a pre-tested recovery plan.

codeExample.code:
az site-recovery vault create \
  --resource-group myRG --vault-name myASRVault \
  --location eastus
# Enable replication via portal or PowerShell after vault creation

words.etymology: From 'site' (a data center or region) + 'recovery' (restoring operations); the service originated as Hyper-V Recovery Manager in 2012.
